Any problems with that one?

Yes and No. Yes I had problems, but it was my own fault. I dropped an O-ring without noticing and when I put it together, I ended up cracking the threads on one of the fittings. They send me a new fitting and O-ring and it works fine now.
My only negative towards it is the amount of pressure required to use it. I have my working pressure set to 40psi. With the working pressure being so high, It's hard to fine tune.

Is there any differences from the regular glass diffusers and the in-line ones?

Yes and No.
Yes in the sense that one is releasing the Co2 directly into the tank and it floats around before getting to the surface and popping. Releasing whatever Co2 was left into the air rather than into the tank. The Inline goes through the propeller in the canister pump and than goes through all the media before reaching the tank. All that turbulence and gong through the media ends up A) exposing it longer to water for absorption, and 2) going through the impeller and filter media causes it to break up so the bubble get smaller and smaller and are absorbed faster. Some people use Co2 Reactors as well as diffusers to prolong the exposure to the water so they get 100% absorption and don't lose any to the surface.
No in the sense that they both function under the same principle. The Co2 is pressurized and forged through almost microscopic holes forcing the gas to be broken apart into mist almost. Both diffusers are doing the same thing. One is glass and the other are ceramic. The process is the same for both.

What kind of equipment/brands do you use as far as regulator,

There are thousands of configurations for regulators. From small regs that use the 12gram BB gun Co2. Slightly larger Paintball tank regs and up to the full size welding regs.. The brands are all over the place. You can get simple regs like the Milwaukee in the last link, up to super fancy Regs like these custom ones that people build. The important thing when buying or building is Single Stage vs Dual Stage. You will want a dual stage reg and here is why. When the Co2 tank pressure drops below your operating pressure, the gas that is left in the tank will "Dump" into the aquarium. Which is usually deadly to your fish. A dual stage reg provides a constant outlet pressure regardless of the decreasing pressure from the inlet on the tank side.
If you can afford to buy a custom built one from someone on the barreport.com or plantedtank.net, you will have a high quality reg. If you want cheaper, milwaukee, Aquatek, and AZoo have middle of the road reviews. I haven't seen a cheap reg that is outstanding in performance. Whichever way you go, try to get the Dual Stage version or else pay close attention to the tank pressure if you use the Single Stage.

CO2 checkers

Co2 Checkers or Drop Checkers as they are sometimes called are useful but not needed. They are simply a visual rough estimate. You can purchase any number of kinds. They all do the same thing and most of them use the same solutions.
One thing to take into consideration is that some of the Checkers come with a bottle that has a regent in that you place place a few drops into bowl and than add tank water. Whenever you use tank water, you are going to get a different reading depending on the PH of your water. The way around this fluctuation is to use 4dKH solution. This solution will give you the truest reading of Co2 saturation without actually having to purchase a PH Probe. You can make your own solution or purchase it from various forum members who have made large batches of it.
The reason that I say that it's more of a rough estimate is because even if your checker shows that you are right in the sweet spot on as far as the color, your plants can actually want more than the checker says. Over the course of a couple of day and with constant monitoring, increase the flow of Co2. Increase a little and wait a day and see how your fish react. What you are looking for is the fish gasping at the surface of the water. If they are gasping, that means you have to much Co2 and you need to dial it back a bit.
I have a very heavily planted tank and my checker is Yellow (Danger zone) and the fish are completely content with no signs of stress, and the plants are growing like weeds.
A Checker comes in handy for lightly planted tanks with few fish in it.

and the like.

I'm going to add bubble counter under "and the like" category.
Bubble counters are like drop checkers and have there pros and cons. You don't need them most of the time, but a lot of people like seeing the visual. One of the reasons you might want one is to use it as a reference for later. Say you have your tank all setup with fish and 10 jungle vals in a 20 Gallon tank. Your plants and fish are doing great and you have a Co2 flow rate of 2 bubbles per second (bps). Than something happens. Say you upgrade your tank to a 55 or you a setup another tank tank with more or fewer plants. You can now use that bubble rate, tank size, and plant density to guesstimate how much more or less Co2 you will need to run in the new or larger tank. You immediately get the Co2 into a range where you know what to expect.

We were going to split them between a 10lbs bottle.

You didn't really saying anything in regards to how you where going to split them, but there are all kinds of Co2 Splitters out there. I have a two way and 3 way brass splitter. A splitter is just going to be personal preference and how many splits it needs. I've seen guys do 12 off a tank.

I'm also going to add Needle valves to the list.
There are tons of version and configurations of needle valves. Some are super ultra micro controlled where it takes 30 turn from full open to closed, and some are 2 turns open to closed.
I personally use an alcheapo ebay pneumatic quick disconnect needle valve. I've run diffusers with 10psi up to the currently 40psi without any leaks. Checkout the forums or ask around here and see what you like and how much you are wanting to spend.

Solenoids.
A Solenoid perform an important function. Co2 runs from the regulator through the Solenoid to your needle valve. The function of the Solenoids is to stop Co2 from passing when you turn off your system. Some people run Co2 24/7, which is really just a waste, since most all plants stop using Co2 when the lights are off.
The way most Solenoids work are they are open and allow gas through when they have power to them, and than close and stop the gas from passing when they don't have power. This is the most common and recommended style. They do make some that close then they have power and open when power is turned off. There isn't really a need to use this kind.
Usually a Solenoid is plugged into the a time with the lights, so it will stop the Co2 when the lights go off. If you are buying a Solenoid. Make sure to get one that has a lot of positive reviews and isn't the cheapest one you can find. You want one the won't get stuck open can gas your fish at night or won't close when you lose power.

Co2 Tubing vs Airline tubing. I personally use airline just because of the cost difference. Co2 is corrosive and will make airline tubing brittle. This brittle tubing can crack at the ends causing Co2 to leak into the air.
It takes a long time to get to the point where you have to replace the airline tubing because it's so brittle it can't handle the pressure or it started to crack at the ends.
Co2 Tubing is more costly but is resistive to corrosion.

were going to split them between a 10lbs bottle, do you think that would be alright or should we honestly scale up?

I would step up to a 20lb tank. For two reasons. The first being the cost difference for filling and the initial purchase are only slightly more than the 10lb or 15lb tanks unless you are going to buy new tank.
The second reason is they last longer and so cost less in the long run. If you don't mind purchasing used. Hit up Craigslist. They are usually in abundant supply. I paid $40 for my 20lb tank and I currently see for my area, 50lb tanks for $150. You may have to start looking early on for a tank in order to snag one at a good price.
When shopping for a used tank check with hydroponic stores as well. Always check with the seller and ask what the most recent certification stamp is on the tank. Some states use a stick, other states stamp it right on the bottle with a hammer and punch. Co2 tanks have to be hydro tested every 5 years and usually cost about $35 - $50 for the test. Refill locations won't refill your tank if it's outside of the cert date. Use this information when purchasing a tank. If your interested in a tank and it's outside of the 5 years since it's last test. Use that to talk the price down.

Would it be easier to just give them their own separate tanks?

If the Aquariums are close enough to each other to not make it look like you have tubes running everywhere, than I would definitely use 1 Co2 Tank between the two aquariums.

Is there any way to control how much CO2 the tanks are getting from one tank?

Yes. The Splitters that I talked about earlier will allow you to independently control flow to both aquarium. Keep in mind that along with the splitter, you will have to get each side it's own needle valve.

Also, what about check valves?

I run a check valve on one of the two lines. My 20 Gallon tanks are on a double stand, so the bottom tank ( Which is also running the inline diffuser) doesn't need a check valve since the tank is lower then the reg.
I do run a check valve on the top tank though and I've gone through 3 different check valves before I found a brand that actually worked.
Lee Check Valve, these no name brand check valves, and This Deep Blue Check Valve where all junk.
I bought this check valve from Zoro.
The "Cracking Pressure" is 1 PSI which is pretty stiff. I'm quite happy with this. I just wish I could find them for a buck instead of $4.

You will want to run a check valve on your system for this reason. When the solenoid shuts off the Co2, you will have "leak back", where the pressure what was forcing it's way through the diffuser stops, It created a slight vacuum and then the pressure from the water starts forcing it's way up the line. When the system turns back on, you will have a lot of back pressure as the Co2 forces all the water back down the line and through the diffuser.
Those three cheap valves I had all let water leak back to the bubble counter. The Co2 would have to push it all back out which took about 30 minutes and added lot more pressure than if just the gas was going through.
The new check valve that I got works great and stops the gas in the line and maintains that pressure so when the system fires back up, it goes to diffusing within a few minutes.
